title: Dependence of Filipino Young Professionals' Well-being on their Investing Years and Income in the National Capital Region
authors: Dela Cruz, M.A.T.; Jurada, P.H.G.; Recreo, C.R.; Mandigma, M.B.S.; Magbata, E.V.S.
venue: Review of Integrative Business and Economics Research, Vol. 15, Issue 2
tldr: Filipino young professionals aged 25-35 in NCR showed significant positive correlations between financial well-being and both years of investing (r=0.364) and income (r=0.309), with financial behavior as the strongest predictor.
problem_and_motivation: Despite existing literature on financial literacy and investment behavior among young professionals, there is no study specifically examining how income levels and years of investing activities relate to overall financial health for young professionals in the National Capital Region. Understanding these relationships is crucial for designing targeted financial interventions.
approach: Descriptive-correlational research design with 389 young professionals aged 25-35 from NCR.
Survey instrument adapted from CFPB Financial Well-Being Scale, validated by experts, pilot-tested with Cronbach Alpha of 0.964.
Purposive sampling via online Google Forms distributed across Facebook and Instagram from February to March 2024.
Pearson correlation coefficient used to measure relationships between variables.
Multiple regression analysis with four models testing combinations of investing years, income, education, and financial behavior as predictors.
findings: num: Overall financial well-being mean score of 3.25 rated as Excellent.
num: Years of investing positively correlates with financial well-being at r=0.364 (p<0.01).
num: Income positively correlates with financial well-being at r=0.309 (p<0.01).
num: Financial behavior is the strongest predictor with standardized beta of 0.706.
num: Full model (investing years, income, financial behavior) explains 62.3% of variance in financial well-being.
num: 39.59% of respondents have 1-2 years of investing experience; 33.16% less than 1 year.
num: 45.24% earn 20,001-50,000 PHP monthly; 25.45% earn 50,001 PHP and above.
key_figures_tables: Table 1: Demographic profile of 389 respondents → 65.04% aged 25-29, 51.93% male, 71.98% single.
Table 2: Investing years and income distribution → majority have 1-2 years investing and earn 20,001-50,000 PHP.
Table 3: Financial well-being items → overall mean of 3.25 classified as Excellent.
Table 4: Correlation analysis → significant positive correlations across all variable pairs at p<0.01.
Table 5: Model summary → Model 4 with financial behavior achieves R-squared of 0.623.
Table 7: Regression coefficients → financial behavior beta=0.706 dominates the model.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This study provides empirical evidence on the financial well-being of Filipino young professionals in the National Capital Region, a demographic underrepresented in financial behavior research. It demonstrates that while years of investing and income positively correlate with financial well-being, financial behavior is the dominant predictor, explaining 62.3% of variance when combined with other factors. The research fills a gap in understanding how investment experience and income interact within the Philippine urban context. It offers a validated instrument (CFPB scale) for measuring financial well-being among Filipino young professionals and establishes baseline metrics for future longitudinal studies.

limits: Cross-sectional design prevents causal inferences between variables.
Purposive sampling limits generalizability beyond NCR young professionals.
Self-reported data may introduce response bias.
Qualitative insights into underlying financial decision-making mechanisms were not gathered.
Long-term tracking of how financial well-being evolves with continued investing was not conducted.
topic_relevance.topic_relevance: All 14 topic domains were systematically scanned. Domain 1 (Filipino Young Professionals) was flagged as high relevance across all three subtopics: 1.A (demographic profile), 1.B (financial structure including income and investing years), and 1.C (financial behavior as a predictor). Domains 4.A and 4.B received low relevance due to brief discussion of existing financial systems and their gaps in serving young professionals. Domains 2, 3, 5-14 were considered and rejected: the paper does not address culturally specific financial practices, expense categorization, behavioral profiling, predictive modeling, budgeting strategies, anomaly detection, mobile design, privacy, engagement, evaluation frameworks, savings/debt management, or synthetic data generation. The paper's primary contribution is demographic financial well-being characterization rather than system design or algorithmic innovation.

limitations: Cross-sectional design prevents causal inferences between variables.
Purposive sampling via social media limits generalizability beyond NCR young professionals.
Self-reported survey data may introduce social desirability and recall bias.
Qualitative insights into underlying financial decision-making mechanisms were not gathered.
Long-term tracking of financial well-being evolution with continued investing was not conducted. [unacknowledged]
